items.title: Front Range voters will decide whether to tax themselves for a train to Pueblo. What Issue 7A would buy
items.summary: A first phase of trains between Denver and Fort Collins is already funded for 2029. Issue 7A would pay for more frequent service and an extension south to Pueblo. A ballot mix-up means hundreds of thousands of people received a question they cannot vote on.

items.title: U.S. measles cases passed 4,000 this year. In November, health officials decide whether the country is still measles-free
items.summary: The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000. A record year of outbreaks, linked chains of transmission dating to January 2025, and a regional review next month could end that status. The protection available to families has not changed.

items.title: Europe's border check now takes your fingerprints. The travel authorization is still coming. What Americans need to know
items.summary: Visitors from outside the EU are now registered with a face scan and fingerprints on their first trip into the Schengen area. The separate online travel authorization, ETIAS, has slipped again. Here is what applies now, what does not, and how to avoid the worst queues.

items.title: International visitors now pay $100 extra at 11 national parks, including Rocky Mountain. How the fee works
items.summary: The surcharge applies at the parks that draw the most foreign visitors, from Yellowstone to Rocky Mountain. For travelers it changes the math of a road trip. For gateway towns that depend on international guests, it adds a cost at the entrance.

items.title: Medicare open enrollment starts October 15. The drug cap is rising, some prices are falling, and your plan may have changed
items.summary: For 2027 the most anyone pays out of pocket for covered Part D drugs goes up by $300, while negotiated prices take effect on a second group of drugs, including semaglutide. The only way to know what it means for you is to compare plans.

items.title: The 1099 threshold is now $2,000 and bonus depreciation is back at 100%. A year-end checklist for owners
items.summary: Two changes from last year's federal tax law land on small businesses this filing season: fewer contractor forms, and an immediate write-off for most equipment. Neither happens automatically in your software, and one depends on what you put in service before the year ends.

items.title: The Supreme Court struck down the emergency tariffs. Getting the money back is a separate fight
items.summary: Roughly $166 billion in duties was collected under the emergency-powers tariffs the Court invalidated in February. Refunds depend on filing, on the status of each entry, and on an appeal that is still running. Small importers have the most to lose by waiting.

items.title: The Fed raised rates for the first time since 2023. What a quarter point means for small business borrowing
items.summary: A unanimous vote, a new chair's first hike, and a signal that one more is likely before year-end. For businesses that borrow on variable rates, the effect shows up quickly. For those with fixed-rate debt, the bigger question is what comes next.

items.title: Colorado scrapped its landmark AI law and wrote a narrower one. Here is what businesses will owe consumers in 2027
items.summary: The 2024 Colorado AI Act never took effect. Its replacement drops impact assessments and the duty of care, and focuses instead on telling people when software helped decide their loan, lease or job, and letting them push back.

items.title: Europe delayed its high-risk AI rules. The transparency rules arrived on schedule anyway
items.summary: The Digital Omnibus on AI moved the hardest compliance deadlines by more than a year. It left the obligations themselves in place, and it did not touch the disclosure duties that now apply to chatbots, deepfakes and AI-generated text.

items.title: Home users got another free year of Windows 10 security updates. Businesses did not. Here is the difference
items.summary: Year one of Windows 10's paid safety net ends October 13. Microsoft quietly gave home PCs a free extension; company-managed machines move to a price that doubles. Many small businesses sit awkwardly between the two.

items.title: COP31 opens in Antalya next month with two presidencies and an unfinished fight over fossil fuels
items.summary: Türkiye hosts, Australia runs the talks, and the Pacific gets a pre-summit stage. Behind the unusual arrangement sit the same questions Belém left open: how to plan an exit from fossil fuels, and who pays for adaptation.

items.title: The Peace Prize goes to Navi Pillay. The committee says the real subject is international law under strain
items.summary: A South African lawyer who sat on the Rwanda tribunal and the International Criminal Court, then led the UN's human rights office, is this year's laureate. The Norwegian Nobel Committee framed the choice as a message about the international legal system itself.

items.title: A telescope made of Antarctic ice wins the physics Nobel. What IceCube found, and why neutrinos matter
items.summary: Neutrinos pass through almost everything, which makes them hard to catch and valuable once caught. Francis Halzen spent decades arguing that a cubic kilometer of polar ice could catch them. This year's prize says he was right.

items.title: The medicine Nobel rewards a way to switch brain cells on with light. Here is how optogenetics works
items.summary: A protein that lets pond algae steer toward sunlight became one of neuroscience's most widely used tools. Three scientists who turned it into a switch for nerve cells share this year's prize in physiology or medicine.

items.title: Monitored wildlife populations are down 73% since 1970. This year’s report leans on the recoveries
items.summary: The headline figure matches the last edition, now extended to 2022. The emphasis has shifted: WWF wants readers to see that targeted conservation is working, and that energy, food and finance decide the rest.

items.title: WHO’s first global rules for treating childhood obesity put lifestyle first and limit drugs to teens
items.summary: About 170 million children and adolescents were living with obesity in 2024. The new guidance treats obesity as a chronic disease, leads with structured lifestyle programs, and draws a firm line on medicines for younger children.

items.title: The chemistry Nobel goes to the scientists who showed how molecules pick a side
items.summary: Many molecules come in left- and right-handed forms, and life uses only one. Two chemists, working a decade apart, showed how a tiny imbalance between those forms can be amplified, work now used in designing reactions for drug manufacturing.

items.title: Samsung’s quarterly profit just topped 100 trillion won. The AI memory boom paid for it
items.summary: Preliminary figures show operating profit up 783% from a year earlier on surging demand for the memory that AI data centers run on. The same price spike is quietly raising costs elsewhere.

items.title: Free AI agents are everywhere now. When does a business need one built to fit?
items.summary: The platforms are giving away general-purpose agents. The work that actually saves a small business time usually lives in the gaps between its own systems, and that is where custom builds earn their keep.

items.title: Meta just handed small businesses a free AI agent. Here is what Muse can touch, and what it cannot
items.summary: Muse for Small Business connects to the tools owners already use and drafts the plans, campaigns and emails they never have time for. The free tier is the headline. The permissions are the story.

items.title: The FTC is investigating rogue AI agents. Businesses deploying them should read the subtext
items.summary: The first U.S. regulatory action aimed squarely at autonomous AI agents targets the labs that build them. The theory behind it, that people and companies answer for what their software does, reaches much further.

items.title: A free national business directory built on open map data, not scraped listings
items.summary: Most directories either scrape other directories or charge businesses to exist. USABusinessSearch.com starts from open map data, lists businesses free, and lets owners claim and correct their own records.

items.title: The White House renamed AI “Super Intelligence.” Here is what actually changes for business
items.summary: A terminology order, a federal definition still to come, and a voluntary accord signed by the biggest model builders. The practical footprint is narrower than the headlines, but it is not zero.

items.title: Rent, buy or subscribe to own: the real cost of a small business website
items.summary: The sticker price of a website tells you very little. What matters is what you pay over the life of the site, what you own at the end of it, and who is accountable when it does not perform.

items.title: SBA disaster loans, explained for small business owners who have never needed one
items.summary: After a declared disaster, the federal government’s largest source of recovery money for businesses is a loan, not a grant. Here is how it works, what it covers and why waiting for the insurance check is the most common mistake.

items.title: A press release written for the machines that now decide who gets quoted
items.summary: Traditional wires sell reach to newsrooms. A newer kind of wire sells something narrower and, for small companies, often more useful: a permanent, dated, attributed record that search engines and AI systems can read without guessing.

items.title: Losing weight on a GLP-1? The muscle you keep matters as much as the pounds you lose
items.summary: The newest weight-loss medications work. The body-composition data from their trials also shows a cost that is easy to miss on a bathroom scale, and the research on how to limit it is getting clearer.

items.title: More than one in four U.S. workers now fear technology will make their job obsolete
items.summary: Gallup’s latest reading is a record, and the worry has moved into groups that used to feel insulated. For employers, the anxiety is now a management problem whether or not the layoffs ever arrive.

items.title: The data center backlash has found its issue: the electricity bill
items.summary: Local fights over hyperscale facilities used to be about noise and land. Now they are about household power costs, and the opposition no longer sorts neatly by party.

items.title: Bathroom remodeling for elderly parents: the aging-in-place decisions that matter most
items.summary: Searches for senior bathroom remodels have jumped this year, and for good reason. The bathroom is where small design decisions have the largest effect on whether someone can keep living at home.

items.title: AI search optimization: how a small business gets named inside the answer
items.summary: Search used to send people to a list of links. Increasingly it hands them a finished answer. For local and small businesses, the job has shifted from ranking on a page to being one of the few names an AI system is willing to cite.

items.title: AI shopping agents can now complete the purchase. Most small stores are not ready to be chosen
items.summary: Checkout inside a chat window has been live for a year, and payment platforms have quietly switched agent support on for millions of merchants. The new problem is not access. It is whether an agent can read your store well enough to pick it.

items.title: The world’s first walk-in VR shopping mall opens its doors
items.summary: World VR Mall lets shoppers walk a three-dimensional concourse and step into storefronts that route through to live ecommerce sites.

items.title: A browser-based flight simulator aimed at student pilots launches without a download
items.summary: No install, no headset, no client. The pitch is procedural familiarity before you start paying for airtime.

items.title: The press release didn’t die. It got rebuilt for machines that read
items.summary: Wire distribution collapsed as an SEO tactic. The format underneath suits machine retrieval almost perfectly.

items.title: The quiet distribution channel: what happens inside local buy-sell groups
items.summary: Community commerce networks move real volume and almost nobody measures them properly.

items.title: Marketing inside the most scrutinized category in medicine
items.summary: What a compliant acquisition strategy looks like when most of the usual channels say no by default.

items.title: Conversational AI has quietly become table stakes for small business websites
items.summary: The demos are easy and the deployments are not. What separates an assistant that earns its place from one that gets switched off.
